"We have faced significantly more hostility and significantly more hate — including death threats," JSUD chairman Ron Dekel told the RND media group. The students blocked Hans-Thomas Tillschneider at an event marking seven years since the antisemitic attack on the synagogue. Dekel defended the action, saying right-wing extremists had no place at a synagogue, particularly when survivors and victims' relatives were mourning. The far-right AfD is classified as extremist in Saxony-Anhalt, where Halle is located and where the party won September's state election. Tillschneider, a deputy speaker of the state parliament, criticized the students and said he had never opposed Jewish life. The legislation still needs approval from the Bundesrat, which represents Germany's states. Lawmakers from the governing conservatives and center-left Social Democrats (SPD) hailed the decision as historic. Michael Thews of the SPD said it would help many people build adequate retirement savings. Fritz Güntzler, finance spokesperson for the center-right Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), said the scheme would also introduce young people to the opportunities offered by capital markets. Opposition lawmakers argued that it would deepen inequality because parents and grandparents can contribute up to €6,840 ($7,500) a year. Stefan Schmidt of the environmentalist Greens called it a two-tier system, saying children who won the "parent lottery" could gain far more than a modest start to retirement saving. The scheme is part of the government's broader pension reform agenda as Germany's aging population puts pressure on the state retirement system.
